youtube.baslik: Vestibular Rehab Exercises: Adapt, Habituate, Substitute | Lesson 259 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Vestibular rehabilitation is made up of gaze stabilization, habituation, substitution, balance and gait exercises. In this lesson we cover VOR x1 and VOR x2 exercises, how exercises are progressed, habituation for motion and visual sensitivity, substitution strategies, balance and gait training, and the dosage recommendations of the current guideline, with examples for educational purposes.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Hall et al., Vestibular rehabilitation for peripheral vestibular hypofunction: an updated clinical practice guideline from the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association, Journal of Neurologic Physical Therapy (2022); Herdman and Clendaniel, Vestibular Rehabilitation; Jacobson and Shepard, Balance Function Assessment and Management; Smith-Wheelock, Shepard and Telian, Physical therapy program for vestibular rehabilitation, American Journal of Otology (1991).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the core exercises of vestibular rehabilitation: gaze stabilization, habituation, substitution and balance.
The exercise examples are for education; each person's program is planned individually by the qualified clinician who assessed them.

cumleler.yazi: The first vestibular exercises were developed by Cawthorne and Cooksey in the 1940s to reduce dizziness brought on by movement.
cumleler.ses: The first vestibular exercises were developed by Cawthorne and Cooksey in the nineteen forties to reduce dizziness brought on by movement.

cumleler: Today, vestibular rehabilitation is made up of four components, chosen according to the problems found in assessment.
The first is gaze stabilization exercises, which aim to keep the image clear during head movement.
The second is habituation exercises, which gradually accustom the person to movements and visual settings that trigger symptoms.
The third is exercises that improve standing and walking balance under different sensory conditions.
The fourth is a walking program that builds general fitness and endurance.

cumleler.yazi: The 2022 American Physical Therapy Association guideline backs this approach in unilateral and bilateral loss with strong evidence.
cumleler.ses: The twenty twenty two American Physical Therapy Association guideline backs this approach in unilateral and bilateral loss with strong evidence.

maddeler.metin: Central signs: refer to a physician

cumleler: The exercise program is planned by a qualified clinician after the cause of dizziness has been found and the person assessed.
If benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is present, repositioning maneuvers come first; exercise does not replace them.
If there are new central signs or unexplained worsening, a medical evaluation is requested instead of exercise.
Because of fall risk, exercises are done in a corner, next to a sturdy chair or countertop.
Mild to moderate dizziness during exercise is expected and acceptable; it should settle quickly.
If severe nausea or long-lasting symptoms occur, intensity is reduced and the clinician is informed.

cumleler.yazi: The basic adaptation exercise for gaze stabilization is VOR x1, built on the vestibulo-ocular reflex, or VOR.
cumleler.ses: The basic adaptation exercise for gaze stabilization is VOR times one, built on the vestibulo-ocular reflex, or VOR.

cumleler: The person looks at a letter on a card at arm's length and turns the head side to side through a small angle.
The target stays still; the head moves as fast as possible while the letter stays clear.
The exercise is kept up for, say, one to two minutes; duration and speed are adjusted to the person's condition.
The same exercise is then repeated moving the head up and down.
If the letter blurs, the head slows down; the aim is to raise the speed over time while keeping the image clear.
By creating retinal slip, this exercise prompts the cerebellum to readjust VOR gain.

notlar.metin: Duration: _For example, one to two minutes_

cumleler.yazi: In the VOR x1 exercise, the target is still and only the head moves.
cumleler.ses: In the VOR times one exercise, the target is still and only the head moves.

cumleler: In this case, the eye must turn in the opposite direction at the same speed as the head; that is, the required gain is one.

cumleler.yazi: In the VOR x2 exercise, the person holds the card and moves it in the direction opposite to the head.
cumleler.ses: In the VOR times two exercise, the person holds the card and moves it in the direction opposite to the head.

cumleler: This time the eye has to turn at twice the head speed; so the exercise is harder.

cumleler.yazi: The program usually starts with VOR x1, and VOR x2 is added as the person progresses.
cumleler.ses: The program usually starts with VOR times one, and VOR times two is added as the person progresses.

cumleler: Both exercises can be done with near and far targets.
As the person becomes comfortable, the speed of head movement is increased first.
The duration of the exercise and the number of repetitions per day are also increased gradually.
The background behind the target can be changed from a plain wall to a patterned or moving background.
The exercise is done first sitting, then standing and finally while walking.
For standing exercises, the surface can change from firm to soft, and the base of support from wide to narrow.
Only one variable is made harder at a time; that way, it is clear why symptoms increase.
Substitution exercises teach other ways to make up for missing information, especially in people with very reduced vestibular function.
In one example, the person moves the eyes to a target first, then turns the head the same way while keeping the eyes on the target.
In another, the person looks at a target, closes the eyes, turns the head and tries to keep the eyes on the remembered target.
These exercises aim to develop preprogrammed eye movements and corrective saccades.
For balance, the aim is to make better use of information from vision and the soles of the feet.
In bilateral vestibulopathy, night lighting and, if needed, supports such as a cane are also part of the substitution strategy.
Herdman and colleagues showed that in bilateral loss, visual acuity during head movement can improve with exercise.
The current guideline states that saccade or smooth pursuit eye exercises without head movement are not recommended for gaze stabilization.
This is because the error signal needed for VOR adaptation is retinal slip that occurs while the head is moving.
The guideline gives this as a strong recommendation.
Eye movements become meaningful when used together with head movement, as in substitution exercises.
So old home program lists made up only of eye exercises should be updated.
Habituation exercises aim to reduce dizziness triggered by specific movements.
First, the movements that cause symptoms are identified, using tools such as the motion sensitivity test with sixteen movements.
Two or three movements that trigger mild to moderate symptoms are chosen.
The person repeats these movements several times a day, enough to bring on symptoms but at a tolerable level.
In this example, the symptom score for a chosen movement decreases gradually over the weeks.
Over time, the brain reduces its response to a stimulus that is repeated and found to be harmless.
Brandt-Daroff exercises were also first described as a habituation exercise.
In some people, symptoms are triggered more by moving or complex visual settings than by head movement.
For these people, optokinetic stimuli such as moving stripes or patterns can be used gradually.
Videos of challenging settings, such as a supermarket aisle or a busy street, are also used for habituation.
Virtual reality settings allow the speed and complexity of the stimulus to be adjusted step by step.
The stimulus can be combined with balance training by presenting it while the person stands or walks.
This approach is especially important in the visual dependence we saw in the lesson on persistent postural-perceptual dizziness.
Balance exercises train the three senses that maintain balance to work together and flexibly.
The base of support is narrowed from wide to narrow: feet apart, feet together, one foot in front, and on one foot.
Going from eyes open to eyes closed removes visual information, and vestibular and body sense information come to the fore.
Moving from a firm surface to a soft one, such as foam, reduces information from the soles of the feet.
Dynamic tasks such as shifting weight forward, back and to the sides, and reaching, are also added.
The right combination of these challenges is chosen according to the situations the person finds hard in daily life.
Exercises are always done in a place safe from falls and, if needed, under supervision.

adimlar.metin: Side to side, up and down

cumleler: In gait training, the person turns the head side to side and up and down while walking; this especially challenges the vestibular system.
Speeding up, slowing down, sudden stops and turns are added.
Tasks such as stepping over or walking around an obstacle create challenges close to daily life.
A second task while walking, such as counting backward or talking, mimics real situations where attention is divided.
At a later stage, walking is practiced outdoors, on grass, sand or in crowds.
In addition, a regular walking program of gradually increasing duration is recommended to build endurance.
The guideline's dosage recommendations are weak recommendations or expert opinion, and are given as minimum levels.
In acute and subacute unilateral loss, gaze exercises can be done at least three times a day, for a total of at least twelve minutes.
For this period, the guideline states that no specific dose can be recommended for balance exercises.
In chronic unilateral loss, gaze exercises are advised three to five times a day, at least twenty minutes in total, for four to six weeks.
In the same group, balance and gait exercises are also recommended for at least twenty minutes a day, for at least four to six weeks.
In bilateral loss, gaze exercises are advised three to five times a day, twenty to forty minutes in total, for about five to seven weeks.
In the same group, a duration of six to nine weeks is recommended for balance exercises, based on expert opinion.
These recommendations come from studies combining weekly clinic visits with a home program.

sahneler.metin: Keep the home program short: two or three exercises, clear duration and repetitions. Write down that symptoms should settle quickly and when to call.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: rather than giving many exercises at once in the home program, start with two or three.
Give the duration, daily repetitions and way to progress each exercise in writing.
Explain that mild dizziness during exercise is expected, but that it should settle quickly.
Make sure the person has a way to reach the clinician if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.

cumleler.yazi: Gaze stabilization exercises train keeping the target clear during head movement; they start with VOR x1 and progress with VOR x2.
cumleler.ses: Gaze stabilization exercises train keeping the target clear during head movement; they start with VOR times one and progress with VOR times two.

cumleler: Habituation exercises rely on repeated exposure, at a tolerable level, to the movements and visual settings that trigger symptoms.
Substitution and balance exercises teach making up for missing vestibular information with vision, body sense and new eye-head strategies.
Eye exercises without head movement are not recommended; the program follows the qualified clinician's individual plan.

sahneler.soru: How does the target move in the VOR x2 exercise?
secenekler: The same way as the head
sahneler.aciklama: The target moves _opposite to the head_; the eye must turn at twice the head speed.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: how does the target move in the VOR x2 exercise?
cumleler.ses: Test yourself: how does the target move in the VOR times two exercise?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: opposite to the head.

cumleler.yazi: The eye then has to turn at twice the head speed; so VOR x2 is harder than VOR x1.
cumleler.ses: The eye then has to turn at twice the head speed; so VOR times two is harder than VOR times one.
